justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across the three time horizons, starting near 137.5 for the one-day forecast and rising gradually to 139.0 at one month. This gentle positive slope was driven primarily by the assumption of a stable or mildly bullish near-term trend, likely anchored to recent price momentum, prevailing macroeconomic conditions such as interest rate expectations, and the general tendency of equity or asset prices to drift slightly higher over short horizons in the absence of strong negative catalysts. The one-day estimate is closely tied to the most recent observed price level, while the one-week and one-month estimates incorporate a small drift premium reflecting longer-horizon mean reversion tendencies and any underlying growth assumptions baked into the asset's recent behavior.

The confidence interval widths expand significantly as the horizon lengthens, which is standard for probabilistic forecasting under uncertainty. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 6.6 units, reflecting the relatively low volatility expected over a single trading session under normal market conditions. By one week, that spread widens to 13 units, and at one month it reaches 26 units, roughly doubling at each step. This scaling reflects the square-root-of-time rule that governs diffusion-based price processes, combined with model uncertainty about whether current volatility regimes will persist. Intraday noise, bid-ask dynamics, and short-term liquidity conditions primarily drive the near-term uncertainty, while macroeconomic data releases, earnings announcements, and shifting risk sentiment dominate the longer-horizon uncertainty.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected negative macro shock — such as a surprise inflation print, an abrupt policy shift from a central bank, or a geopolitical escalation — could drive prices well below the lower bounds, particularly over the one-week and one-month horizons. Liquidity crises or sudden risk-off episodes have historically produced moves far larger than standard volatility models anticipate. On the upside, a positive catalyst such as better-than-expected earnings, a dovish policy surprise, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical uncertainty could push prices above my upper bounds. These tail events are precisely why stated 90% intervals, by construction, leave a 10% probability mass in the combined tails, and real-world fat-tailed distributions mean the actual tail risk may be modestly larger than my intervals imply.
